props.title: The General
props.initialSlug: Civil War hero risks all to rescue train & love

sections.content: Buster Keaton's **The General** (1926) represents the absolute peak of silent-era physical comedy and technical innovation. Shot with real trains on actual railroad tracks, Keaton performed death-defying stunts while telling a Civil War story based on a true incident. The film's most famous sequence - a real locomotive crashing through a burning bridge into a river - was the most expensive single shot in silent film history. Keaton's deadpan performance style, nicknamed "The Great Stone Face," influenced generations of comedic actors from Bill Murray to Jackie Chan.

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond comedy. Modern action directors like Christopher Nolan studied **The General** (1926) for its practical effects and precise visual storytelling. The chase sequences, shot with multiple cameras on parallel train tracks, established techniques still used in action films today. **Mad Max: Fury Road** (2015) director George Miller cited Keaton's work as a major influence on his own vehicular action sequences.

While contemporary audiences in 1926 didn't fully embrace the film, likely due to its Civil War setting and ambitious budget, **The General** (1926) has been vindicated by history. Orson Welles called it "the greatest comedy ever made, the greatest Civil War film ever made, and perhaps the greatest film ever made." Its combination of epic scope, technical innovation, and perfectly-timed physical comedy remains unmatched. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Silent Action-Comedy

sections.content: **The General** (1926) established a template for action-comedy that resonates through film history. Jackie Chan's blend of death-defying stunts and precise comic timing in films like **Project A** (1983) and **Police Story** (1985) directly channels Keaton's approach. Modern filmmakers continue drawing from Keaton's practical effects playbook - **Mission: Impossible - Dead Reckoning Part One** (2023) features Tom Cruise performing real train stunts that echo Keaton's work.
